title: What are urban explorers?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss urban exploration: visiting and documenting abandoned structures, its origins with the San Francisco group Suicide Club in the 1970s (with MIT steam tunnel exploring in the 1950s as an earlier precedent), the codes of conduct (take only pictures, leave only footprints), documentation online via Flickr and sites like Forgotten Detroit and UER, personal exploration stories (Fort Pickens in Florida, an Atlanta warehouse with old MARTA blueprints, an abandoned Evandale mall), the dangers and illegality of trespassing, and destination sites such as Danvers State Hospital and Waverly Hills Sanatorium in Kentucky. The episode ends with listener mail correcting an episode on the JFK assassination (Texas Governor John Connally was in the car) and a clarification on prescription Tylenol with Codeine versus over-the-counter Tylenol.
topics: take only pictures leave only footprints

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with casual banter about an old closed store and the appeal of peering into empty buildings, then introduce the topic of urban exploration.

segments.title: Definition and history of urban exploration
segments.summary: Urban exploration is defined as visiting and exploring abandoned or neglected man-made structures, not necessarily urban. It began in earnest in 1970s San Francisco with the group Suicide Club, who toured utility tunnels and hospitals and jumped into the bay during storms. Earlier precedent: MIT students touring steam tunnels in the 1950s. The hobby took about twenty years to catch on, and the Internet helped it grow.

segments.title: Codes of conduct and respect for sites
segments.summary: Urban explorers follow a strict code of conduct: take nothing, break nothing, and leave only footprints. They contend with homeless people using buildings for shelter and vandals who spray graffiti. An explorer who found a 19th-century mining office read personnel files and returned them without taking anything.
topics: take only pictures leave only footprints

segments.title: Documenting exploration online
segments.summary: Because explorers can't take things, they document their finds with photos. Flickr searches and websites such as Forgotten Detroit and the Canadian site UER host exploration photos. Documentation captures decaying places before they are demolished.

segments.title: Personal exploration stories
segments.summary: Josh describes childhood barn exploring in Georgia and a teenage trip to Fort Pickens in Florida with torches, where they explored Civil War-era rooms and tunnels. Years later in Atlanta he found old MARTA subway blueprints in an empty warehouse. Chuck describes exploring an abandoned Evandale mall in Atlanta, now demolished. The hosts discuss the thrill of large empty buildings.

segments.title: Dangers, legality and destination sites
segments.summary: The hosts say they do not recommend urban exploring because it is trespassing and dangerous, since building inspectors only inspect functioning buildings. An Australian drowning in a sewer storm is mentioned. They discuss destination sites: Danvers State Hospital (featured in the movie Session Nine) and Waverly Hills Sanatorium in Kentucky, which is open for tours despite being a former tuberculosis hospital.

segments.title: Listener mail corrections
segments.summary: Corrections: Texas Governor John Connally was in the car with JFK, not a senator as stated earlier. Carrie Clinger, a dentist, explains that prescription Tylenol with Codeine is a narcotic and differs from over-the-counter Tylenol, so it is regulated.
